<1>Personal integrity</1>

Beyond functional utility, the IOC projects a layer of personal integrity and symbolic identity, because the user's position in the ecosystem is produced by regimes of visibility, recognition and belonging. The task now is to define relevant losses that can be neither downgraded to “displeasure” nor treated as a side effect. In digital ecosystems, the value offered and enjoyed is not exhausted by instrumental utilities, because it depends on regimes of visibility, recognition, belonging and reputation that <1>p. 457</1> form part of the very experience of enjoyment and condition the subject's practical position in the environment.

For this reason, the dogmatic reconstruction of the immaterial object of consumption must incorporate, as a dimension of relevant loss, the consumer's personal integrity and symbolic identity, understood as functional components of enjoyment in private spaces that operate, to a large extent, as environments of social participation and status projection. The problem is to make them legally tractable through objective delimitations and criteria of controllability, including in order to capture losses that affect the enjoyment bundle even when there is no total interruption, but rather a persistent downgrading of the conditions of use and recognition.

In Reale's thought, this type of construction is neither an arbitrary gesture nor a later moralization by the interpreter. The legal norm operates as an integration of facts and values, without being reduced to an empty logical form and without being confused with a mechanical reflection of the world. It is this integration that authorizes treating platform-governed enjoyment as a legally modelable experience, because “the normative structures, which constitute Objective Law, are not mere empty logical forms, but forms of a concrete experience, whose dominant or essential lines were abstracted from social reality to operate as an instrument of social discipline, that is, as ‘legal models’” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 1994, p. 109- 110)</2>.

In scenarios of technical mutation, legal meaning may shift without the response depending on moral rhetoric, since “an unforeseen circumstance of a technical order can completely alter the signification and content of a legal text” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 164)</2>. This adjustment remains controllable because valuation and decision remain bound to facts and values, imposing methodological limits against voluntarism. With this grounding, personal integrity and symbolic identity can be formulated as functional dimensions of supply in digital ecosystems, provided they are defined by criteria of relevance and verifiability that preserve decidability.

Personal integrity, in the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, designates neither an emotional state nor subjective discomfort arising from ordinary market frustrations. It designates the preservation of minimum conditions of agency, continuity and practical orientation of the consumer within a technical-organizational environment that permanently manages the possibilities of enjoyment. When the acquired utility is realized as a position of enjoyment sustained by a platform, the subject is not merely the recipient of content, but a participant in an ecosystem that organizes access, priorities, visibilities and sanctions.

<1>p. 458</1> Integrity is affected when these conditions are downgraded persistently or structurally, to the point of converting the experience of use into chronic instability, functional disorientation or loss of control over one's own way of existing in the environment, even if formal access remains available. Legal relevance, therefore, lies not in measuring internal disturbances, but in identifying when the continuous management of the environment significantly alters the level of predictability, consistency and governability of enjoyment, eroding the core of utility stabilized in the bond.

This cut only holds if protection is not captured by a resigned empirical description of the functioning of the ecosystem. The counterfactual stabilization of normative expectations, already established as a methodological lock of the IOC regime, is decisive at this point because it makes it possible to affirm normative expectations about continuity, loyalty in performance and preservation of minimum conditions of enjoyment even under opacity and mutability. With this, the persistent downgrading of these conditions can be reconstructed as relevant loss without requiring proof of sociological “normality” nor depending on moral reproach of the technical arrangement.

Dogmatics, however, can only deal with this type of loss if it is able to delimit the phenomenon and make it decidable, avoiding descriptive paralysis in the face of the environment's complexity. Under the technological function already established, dogmatic delimitation operates through a cut in reality that isolates the problems relevant to decision-making <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 92])</2> and organizes uncertainties into a specialized technique compatible with normative binding and with institutional pressure for decision <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 86-87])</4>.

Personal integrity thus ceases to be a subjective appeal and becomes matter that can be delimited by criteria, making it possible to locate typical losses in the gap between formally preserved enjoyment and materially degraded enjoyment. Protection no longer depends on the crude figure of total interruption and comes to reach situations in which access remains nominal, but the experience of use is downgraded by persistent alterations in the conditions of participation, predictability and governability of the environment.

Relevant degradation may take the form of cumulative restrictions, gradual reconfigurations of functionalities, persistent changes in access rules, selective frictions and reiterated instability that makes enjoyment unpredictable or structurally disadvantageous. Even when there is no immediate collapse of access, the aggregate effect may erode the capacity to orient one's own action, plan permanence and exercise use according to stabilizable normative expectations, delimiting the point at which modulation ceases to be <1>p. 459</1> an ordinary variation of supply and comes to constitute a significant downgrading of the enjoyment bundle.

The argument must, then, make explicit that part of the value enjoyed in digital ecosystems is not merely instrumental, but symbolic and socially structured. To that end, it is necessary to set aside the reading that symbolic value is a mere private emotional projection, immune to control and, for that reason, legally irrelevant. Under the semiotic apparatus already established, the sign is not a subjective ornament that accompanies experience, since it operates as a public structure that organizes conduct and produces verifiable social effects, regardless of its physical truth or of individual mental states. In this light, interpretation can be understood as an objective datum, since interpretants, that is, the relations of interpretation, do not necessarily depend on individual mental representations and are collectively verifiable <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 1991, p. 112)</2>.

Under the semiotic lock already established, symbolic identity ceases to be an introspective appeal and comes to designate a socially instituted position in systems of signs that structure expectations, recognition and belonging in the ecosystem. Meaning is not reduced to a mental image, but operates as a relation instituted by the code, and even connotation becomes predictable through a shared lexicon, which makes it possible to describe symbolic losses by public criteria.

Symbolic identity, in the IOC regime, designates the consumer's public position in an ecosystem of signs managed by a platform, in which visibility, reputation, belonging and distinction function as practical conditions of enjoyment and as components of the economically experienced value. This identity is formed and stabilized by socially operative criteria of recognition, frequently coded in metrics, badges, rarities, <1>rankings</1>, participation history, relationship networks and regimes of access to spaces and functionalities. When the utility of the object depends on these mediations, the enjoyment bundle structurally includes the continuity of this position and the possibility of exercising it over time. The platform may formally preserve access to the content and, even so, reconfigure the criteria that define status, reach, belonging and recognition, degrading the socially instituted core of utility that sustained enjoyment as a practice.

An especially didactic example of this symbolic identity as a public position appears in the end-of-season ranked rewards and, in particular, in the “Victorious” <1>skins</1> and in the borders associated with the tier<2><3>460</3></2>. These signs do not operate as mere <4>p. 460</4> cosmetics, because they become social proof immediately legible in the ecosystem, stabilizing a form of reputation that is simultaneously historical and displayable, since the player comes to carry, on the very symbolic body of the account, a mark of performance and temporal dedication recognized by third parties <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2026b)</6>. The consequence is that enjoyment ceases to be merely access to the game and comes to include the permanence of this visible biography as a component of the economically experienced value, because it organizes expectation, distinction and belonging in internal circuits of recognition.

The intelligibility of this public position can also be reinforced by the sociology of sport, insofar as institutionalized competitive practices produce not only performance, but stable forms of community, integration and reciprocal recognition. Helal<1><2>461</2></1> observes that sport is one of the most solid social institutions of the modern world and that its presence deeply penetrates everyday life, influencing habits, customs and modes of social insertion <3>Helal</3><4>(Helal, 1990, p. 11-12; p. 14)</4>. Along the same lines, treating sport as a social fact, the author stresses that it imposes itself on individuals from an early age, so much so that those who do not take to the sport of their social group often experience the condition of the non-integrated, while sporting taste itself is formed in the collectivity, and not as a purely private or spontaneous preference <5>Helal</5><6>(Helal, 1990, p. 12-14)</6>.

This perspective is particularly useful for understanding continuous competitive ecosystems such as that of <1>League of Legends</1><2><3>462</3></2>. When competition is stabilized by seasons, <4>p. 461</4> <5>rankings</5>, rewards, public circuits, shared memory and recognizable signs of prestige, enjoyment no longer consists of a mere succession of matches and comes to operate as insertion into a socially structured space, in which belonging, reputation and biographical continuity are produced collectively. Within this frame, the value of the IOC is not exhausted by the instrumental utility of access, because it includes permanence in a competitive community organized by shared codes, mutual recognition and public criteria of distinction. For this reason, exclusions, persistent restrictions or relevant downgrades of the conditions of participation affect not only the user's functional conveniences, but may bear directly on their symbolic identity and on the continuity of their socially recognized position in the ecosystem.

This same arrangement makes clear why symbolic identity, when institutionalized by a platform, can produce identity captivity. Obtaining the sign of prestige depends not only on competitive performance, but also on maintaining a state of eligibility managed by disciplinary technologies of conduct, in which low Honor levels bar the player from seasonal rewards <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025a)</2><3><4>463</4></3>. In this dynamic, the subject comes to manage their own behavior with a view to preserving recognition and narrative continuity, because the relevant threat is not <5>p. 462</5> only the loss of a match or of a functional convenience, but the frustration of a rare reward that consolidates status and that, once missed, cannot simply be repurchased as an equivalent substitute. Conformity ceases to be mere “following the rules” and becomes a mechanism of self-preservation of a socially operative position in the ecosystem, in which the cost of leaving is not limited to time or money, but includes the loss of displayable historicity.

The legal point that this example illuminates is that accumulated symbolic capital is maintained under a regime of disciplined permanence, since the platform not only describes standards of conduct, but reserves to itself a power of intervention capable of downgrading enjoyment through functional limitations, restrictions on interaction, redefinitions of progress and, in extreme cases, the very termination of participation, with measures that may be triggered even when the specific conduct is not previously listed as inappropriate <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2><3><4>464</4></3>. In this way, the risk of sanction bears not only on formal access, but on the integrity of agency and on the maintenance of symbolic identity as a public position, since the system of rewards and eligibility turns prestige into something both desirable and vulnerable to private governance. In practical terms, what the environment recognizes as merit becomes, at the same time, an instrument of capture through disciplinary asymmetry, since preserving the possibility of receiving and sustaining signs of prestige comes to require continuous self-adjustment to administratively controlled criteria and determinations <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2024k)</6><7><8>465</8></7>.

Within this frame, relevant downgrading may consist of loss of position, persistent disqualification, erasure of signs of distinction, systematic instability of <1>p. 463</1> recognition or restrictions that make participation in internal circuits of value unfeasible. Symbolic identity thus functions as a lens that makes visible losses which do not take the form of total interruption, but directly affect the position of enjoyment and its continuity as utility.

Personal integrity and symbolic identity become fully intelligible as dimensions of the IOC when it is recognized that, in platform-governed environments, agency and identity are not located outside supply as mere psychological phenomena, but can be configured by architectural design and by continuous modulation. Cohen synthesizes this point by stating that technologies and artifacts mediate the embodied perception of reality and that, over time, they come to constitute and define the lived world, so that networked information technologies not only empower the networked self, but configure it <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 36])</2>.

This configuration is carried out through layers of protocols and structural choices that simultaneously enable certain flexibilities and block others, while producing legibility and intermediation compatible with the platform's own priorities <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 42)</2>. In the same movement, flows of personal data are refined to produce operational representations of the user, structured to make behaviors calculable, predictable and profitable at scale <3>Cohen</3><4>(Cohen, 2019, p. 67)</4>. The legal consequence is that agency comes to be treated as a governable variable of supply and that motivational patterns can be reinforced in pre-deliberative layers through techniques of choice architecture and algorithmic anticipation <5>Cohen</5><6>(Cohen, 2019, p. 77)</6>. Thus, the enjoyment bundle may include architecturally produced conditions of visibility, recognition and participation, and the degradation of these conditions may constitute relevant loss without depending on the consumer's introspection.

The identification of relevant losses in the IOC can, then, be structured as a matrix that captures the harm without depending on total interruption or subjective assessment. The common axis is the impairment of the position of enjoyment over time, as a combination of practical conditions of use and agency in the environment with conditions of recognition, visibility and belonging that form part of the socially instituted utility.

Relevant losses, in this regime, include exclusion or significant limitation of participation when the platform prevents the normal exercise of the enjoyment bundle through persistent blocks, restrictions or downgrades. They include substantial degradation of the conditions of use when gradual reconfigurations, selective frictions, reiterated instabilities or rule changes erode the predictability and governability of the experience. They include the <1>p. 464</1> devaluation or erasure of signs of distinction and reputation when metrics, badges, rarities, histories or visibility criteria are altered so as to disfigure the stabilized symbolic utility. They include, finally, the structural reconfiguration of access and recognition when the consumer remains within the ecosystem, but durably loses the capacity to occupy the position of enjoyment that made the object economically and socially valuable.

Organized in these terms, the problem ceases to be described as diffuse discomfort and comes to separate ordinary variations of service from significant downgrades of the enjoyment bundle, distinguishing alterations compatible with continued performance from those that transform, to the consumer's detriment, the minimum conditions of agency, participation and recognition that sustained the acquired utility.

The incorporation of symbolic identity as a component of the enjoyment bundle is also sustained because legal rationality assimilates social structures of recognition, roles and history as conditions of coordination and of limitation of meaning. In the sense indicated by Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr., elements such as reputation and stereotypes function as material topoi that can be mobilized in legal discussion, allowing the parties to present themselves as upright people, in good faith, aware of duties and rights and bearers of recognized public merit, in opposition to a minority or to interests described as deviant <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 84)</2>. The same mechanism appears in the idea of role. For the author, assuming a role means becoming entangled in actions that the agent comes to have to represent as part of himself, and this assumption functions as a presupposition of continuous interaction, producing a paradoxical cooperation, since the parties recognize each other as such even in a condition of conflict <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 75)</4>. The communicative situation also delimits meaning through its own history, since generating one's own history means differentiating one's own behavior in reference to the more complex history of the surrounding world. In this dynamic, every behavior that enters the communicative situation contributes to limiting it, because it excludes and enables alternatives and ensures other discursive behaviors <5>Jr.</5><6>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 59)</6>. On platforms, internal positions of user, participant, creator, moderated or sanctioned are equally organized by roles and recognitions that condition enjoyment as a social practice, so that persistent downgrades of status and participation may affect the core of utility even without total interruption of access.

The reference to digital citizenship operates neither as a constitutionalizing shift nor as an inflated metaphor, but as a functional description of the way certain private ecosystems have come to concentrate relevant conditions of social participation, recognition and <1>p. 465</1> circulation of reputation. Consumer relationships structure access to spaces of interaction, mechanisms of visibility and internal circuits of value that, in practice, function as everyday infrastructure of belonging, public exposure and the exercise of social roles. The argument is put in strict terms. The platform operates as a private environment of public relevance insofar as it structures practical opportunities for expression, participation and recognition, and continuous consumption places the consumer in a position of functional dependence on these conditions. Within this frame, private sanctions, reconfigurations of visibility and persistent downgrades cease to be indifferent operational variations when they substantially alter the consumer's capacity to occupy socially relevant positions within the environment, with effects that extend beyond the instrumental use of the service.

For this impairment to be legally assimilable, the content of what is understood here as personal integrity in the IOC regime must be made explicit. The term is employed as an umbrella concept compatible with the theory of quality in the CDC<1><2>466</2></1>, which already operates through categories broad enough to encompass harms arising from the fact of consumption without requiring the crude figure of total interruption or of immediate material injury. Personal integrity includes, therefore, classic dimensions of physical, psychological, patrimonial and even aesthetic integrity, but now also comes to incorporate an operational facet proper to continuous <3>p. 466</3> consumption in an environment. It is integrity as to the capacity for agency and predictability, understood as the minimum set of conditions that allows the consumer to orient their own action, understand practical consequences, plan permanence and exercise use according to stabilizable normative expectations in an ecosystem governed by architecture and by private sanctions.

This integrity of agency does not correspond to a private emotional state or to a psychological parameter of protection. It designates a functional condition of existence in the system, observable in patterns of governability of the environment, stability of rules and legibility of consequences. In ecosystems of governed enjoyment, the consumer may remain formally “inside” and, even so, lose control over how they exist in the system, when a regime of chronic instability sets in, produced by repeated alterations of rules, selective frictions, gradual reconfigurations of functionalities, opacification of visibility criteria and unpredictability of sanctions. What deteriorates is the capacity to maintain enjoyment as a practice orientable over time. Relevant loss appears when modulation ceases to be an ordinary variation of supply and comes to persistently erode the possibility of acting with minimum predictability and of sustaining a position of use endowed with practical meaning.

In this same register, symbolic identity and personal integrity are connected by two effects of dependence that can be named symbolic captivity and identity captivity. The first designates the platform's capacity to replace public repertoires of signification with proprietary signs and internal grammars that come to organize value, belonging and recognition, reducing external comparability and reordering the user's interpretable world under managed metrics, rarities, badges, <1>rankings</1> and regimes of visibility. The second designates the form of dependence in which the cost of exit is not exhausted in financial or convenience dimensions, because it implies loss of narrative continuity and of positions of recognition whose existence takes place, decisively, within the ecosystem, through networks, histories, roles and internal circuits of value. In both cases, it is not a matter of hypnosis of the consumer nor of psychologization of the bond, but of a functional description of how architecture, curation and sanction can produce dependence through exit costs and through asymmetry of governance, directly affecting agency and the position of enjoyment.

Fixing a protective core that includes personal integrity, in its facet of agency and predictability, and symbolic identity, as a socially instituted public position, does not stand as a license for axiological voluntarism, but as a <1>p. 467</1> controllable cut anchored in objective requirements of valuation and in structural limits of legal experience itself.

In Reale's thought, the evaluative dimension does not operate as a moral supplement external to Law. Decision-making authority does not detach itself from the axiological horizon that makes normativity intelligible, since the binding force of Law is linked to axiological requirements and to a set of options processed in the social milieu, from which decision-making authority is not separated. Along this line, every norm enunciates something that ought to be because a value was recognized as the determining reason for a behavior declared obligatory <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 33)</2>. When legal experience identifies fundamental values as conditions of possibility of the system itself, valuation takes the form of a limit and not of rhetoric. Reale maintains that, in the dialogical process of history, man becomes aware of certain fundamental values, such as the inviolability of the human person, which, once brought to the light of historical consciousness, come to be considered intangible. For the author, these values act as transcendental axiological constants of Law, since it was they that made legal experience possible <3>Reale</3><4>(Reale, 1994, p. 108)</4>.

Accordingly, the protection of integrity and identity, when operated as functional dimensions of enjoyment in private environments of public relevance, can be formulated as a protective core without abstract moralism, provided it remains bound to criteria of relevance and to standards of verifiability capable of converting this core into decidable losses in the IOC regime.

This incorporation requires, however, explicit delimitation to prevent personal integrity, symbolic identity, symbolic captivity, identity captivity and digital citizenship from turning into expansive labels capable of absorbing any discomfort arising from ordinary market frictions. It is not a matter of elevating the consumer's experience to a psychological parameter or of transforming trivial frustrations, aesthetic preferences or normal fluctuations of service into matters of reinforced protection. Nor is it a matter of attributing unlawfulness to technology as such or of replacing dogmatic criteria with moral reproach of the business model. The cut is functional. In platform-governed enjoyment, part of the economically acquired value depends on architecturally produced conditions of participation, visibility, recognition and governability of the environment, and the relevant degradation of these conditions may objectively affect the enjoyment bundle without taking the form of total interruption. For this reason, the categories only operate when the downgrading is significant and persistent, when it substantially alters the level of agency and the position of the <1>p. 468</1> consumer in the ecosystem, and when it can be described by verifiable criteria of loss in the IOC regime, under the filters of relevance and controllability.

The passage to standards of proof and restoration finally requires making explicit why losses so delimited must be converted into decidable alternatives even when platform governance operates under opacity and mutability. Under the methodological locks already consolidated, legal technique does not suspend its action in the face of opacity, since it organizes criteria to make it bearable under normative binding and institutional pressure for decision, increasing uncertainties in a manner oriented toward action <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 87])</2>.

In this key, the absorption of insecurity justifies transforming initially diffuse losses into controllable cuts, since the act of deciding converts undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives, even if, at a subsequent moment, it generates new incompatibilities, sometimes more complex than the previous ones, without this transformation being confused with a promise of harmony <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 312-313])</2>. The matrix of losses relating to personal integrity and symbolic identity, thus outlined, does not purport to exhaust the phenomenon, but to make it decidable by criteria, opening the way for the formulation of standards of verifiability and restoration compatible with continued enjoyment.

Thus, the protective core outlined for personal integrity and symbolic identity ceases to be a rhetorical ornament and comes to function as an instrument of attribution and restoration compatible with the IOC's mode of existence. Platform-governed enjoyment cannot be read only through the lens of formal access nor through the crude category of total interruption, because what is acquired and lost is frequently a position of enjoyment that is realized over time and under architectural governance. When this position is degraded by persistent reconfigurations of conditions of use, participation, visibility and recognition, relevant loss may occur without collapse of access and, even so, affect the core of utility economically experienced and socially verifiable in the ecosystem. The result is a reading rule that ties together the three planes already opened: the object remains intelligible as an immaterial product, the relevant conduct can be reconstructed in architectural patterns oriented by exploitative purpose, and relevant losses can be described by criteria that capture substantial degradations of the enjoyment bundle, including in its symbolic dimension. This conceptual architecture provides controllable cuts that make decidable what, under abstract labels or narrow categories of defect and interruption, would tend to remain invisible, and prepares the shift of the diagnosis to the <1>standards</1> of proof, control and redress capable of dealing with gradual losses, persistent downgrades and architectural reconfigurations without <2>p. 469</2> requiring total transparency or reducing protection to the binary logic of “works or does not work” or of an object “intact or defective”.

The policy of ranked match rewards per season makes the reward explicit as a conditioned sign and, therefore, as an institutional technology of prestige. The support article on end-of-season rewards is the space where the developer states as an objective requirement that the player “Finish the season with Honor Level 3 or higher” and also “Win 15 ranked matches” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026b)</2>. That is, the reward does not present itself as a neutral item, but as an institutional certification of ranking merit. Something publicly legible through which the platform defines not only what “winning” is, but also what “being recognized” is so that merit is converted into prestige capable of being enjoyed through display. <3>↩</3>

A Doctor of Sociology from <1>New York University</1>, Ronaldo Helal is a Brazilian sociologist and professor at the Faculty of Social Communication and in the Graduate Program in Communication of the State University of Rio de Janeiro (UERJ). His academic trajectory places him among the pioneering names in the consolidation of studies on sport, media and culture in Brazil, which gives special density to the use of his work <2>O que é sociologia do </2> <3>esporte</3> as theoretical support to understand sport not only as a competitive practice, but as a social phenomenon that produces integration, belonging and collective forms of recognition. <4>↩</4>

The relevance of League of Legends to this point does not stem from an isolated historical curiosity, but from its central role in the public and institutional consolidation of e-sports as a socially recognizable competitive practice. A frequently recalled milestone of this process occurred in 2013, when Danny “Shiphtur” Le, a professional League of Legends player, received a P-1A visa in the United States, a category traditionally associated with internationally recognized athletes, in an episode that became a symbol of the institutional recognition of the e-sports competitor as a figure analogous to the professional athlete <1>Dave</1><2>(Dave, 2013)</2>. This fact, by itself, does not exhaust the phenomenon, but helps to situate League of Legends within a broader process of social stabilization of digital competition. Riot itself came to present LoL Esports as a global platform devoted to the game's regional and international competitions, articulating local leagues, global events and integrated digital experiences for the audience, with its own identity and specific governance <3>LOLESPORTS STAFF</3><4>(LoLEsports Staff, 2020)</4>. In parallel, its contemporary structure of competitive operations describes a global ecosystem organized into regional leagues and structured circuits, including at grassroots and semi-professional levels, revealing that these are not sporadic competitions, but a reiterated, documented and regulated order of competitive participation <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2026l)</6>. It is precisely there that the sociology of sport illuminates the legal problem. When a competitive practice is stabilized by calendars, seasons, leagues, rankings, rules of its own, a recurring audience and collective memory, it ceases to be merely a sequence of matches and comes to operate as a social form. In the case of League of Legends, this manifests itself not only in the existence of world championships and regional circuits, but also in the public and ritualized staging of these events. In describing the global broadcast of the 2022 World Championship, Riot reported that the tournament was brought to the public by 22 broadcast partners, in 21 languages, with millions of viewers around the world and a peak of about 70 million people watching the final, which attests to public scale, shared expectation and the production of common memory far beyond the individual use of the game <7>Riot Games</7><8>(Riot Games, 2022p)</8>. The community dimension also appears in the modes of collective following and participation in the competitive scene. Riot itself came to promote and publicize official or authorized watch parties for the World Championship, that is, collective gatherings of spectators organized around the championship, which shows that the competitive ecosystem mobilizes not only players individually considered, but also practices of fandom, conviviality, ritualization and belonging around the game <9>Riot Games</9><10>(Riot Games, 2025t)</10>. For this reason, the utility socially experienced in League of Legends cannot be reduced to technical access to matches. In an environment so structured, remaining in the ecosystem also means keeping a position in a competitive community endowed with its own codes, recognizable distinctions, shared memory and internal circuits of recognition. Exclusion, banning, lasting loss of access or relevant downgrading of the conditions of participation do not affect only the functional use of the service. They may bear on belonging, displayable historicity, reputation and biographical continuity within a socially organized space. It is precisely in this sense that the sociology of sport helps to make legally intelligible the existential and symbolic weight of permanence, participation and exclusion in institutionalized digital competitive ecosystems. <11>↩</11>

The “Honor Guide” makes explicit the link between conduct and access to rewards, converting behavior into a condition of internal citizenship. The document describes the Honor system as “a general reflection of any player's behavior in and out of game” and states that it “rewards sportsmanlike conduct” while at the same time it “penalizes inappropriate behaviors with reduced rewards” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025a)</2>. In the table of benefits, the rule appears in operational form: under “Ranked Season Rewards”, Honor 1 and Honor 2 are listed as “No”, while Honor 3, 4 and 5 are listed as “Yes” (same page). This transforms end-of-season prestige into a mechanism of conformation, because it shifts the problem from “playing well” to “staying compliant” so that merit is institutionally recognized. <3>↩</3>

The User Rules reinforce that the player's position in the ecosystem is subject to a regime of disciplined permanence, with sanctions that affect access, visibility and continuity. The contract states that, to be eligible, the user must comply with “the acceptable use and behavior policies” published by the company and that, in case of violation, Riot may impose “temporary bans, suspension, or termination and deletion of the account”, in addition to “removal of content, resets of user progress”, “limitations on chat functionality” and “restrictions and bans from matchmaking queues”, “regardless of whether a specific behavior is listed or not” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The same passage makes explicit the infrastructure of control by declaring that Riot uses “human moderators” and “technological means, such as automated systems and machine learning tools” to ensure compliance with the rules <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. The issue at hand is not the abstract legitimacy of this discipline, but the structural consequence of its falling upon signs and positions that make up the value enjoyed as symbolic identity. <5>↩</5>

A clear example of how sanction and prestige are connected appears in end-of-season announcements, in which Riot describes conduct that eliminates the player from rewards and, therefore, produces direct loss of symbolic capital. In the text <1>Fim da Temporada 2024 - Etapa 3</1>, Riot states that “Accounts involved in MMR manipulation and manipulative behaviors result in immediate suspension of the accounts, removal of the Honor level and exclusion from the ranked rewards of the season/Split” <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024k)</3>. The sequence is decisive, since the platform not only sets out to punish the account as access, but also resorts to the withdrawal of eligibility and exclusion from rewards, directly affecting the core of recognition and the narrative continuity that structures symbolic identity in the ecosystem. <4>↩</4>

The use of “personal integrity” as an umbrella concept to encompass the binomial “health and safety” native to consumer protection does not propose the creation of a new legal interest, but an operation that engages directly with the dogmatics already stabilized in the CDC. In Claudia Lima Marques's reconstruction, consumer protection in the market is organized, at least, by the protection of their physical and psychological integrity and their economic integrity, in addition to the concern with the moment at which this protection applies in contractual dynamics <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 13)</2>. This frame engages directly with the theory of quality in the CDC, understood as a legal duty of quality-adequacy and quality-safety, by which quality defects due to inadequacy and to lack of safety are qualified according to reasonable expectations of supply, as a functional substitute for the classic categories of the redhibitory defect in the previous regime <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1349)</4>. In this framing, the inclusion of an operational facet linked to agency and predictability in environments of platform-governed enjoyment can be presented as an extension of the adequacy of the supply regime itself, and not as a normative innovation. The recent literature that describes so-called digital vulnerability as the power of commercial actors to affect decisions, desires and behaviors in a way that the consumer tends not to tolerate, but is not in a position to prevent, helps to bring out the reverse of this integrity of agency, as a practical loss of the capacity for orientation and containment of the environment <5>Mucelin</5><6>(Marques; Mucelin, 2022, p. 2)</6>. This loss is associated with a structural, architectural aspect, in which the environment is designed to change behaviors, anticipating biases and operating through digital choice architectures, which reinforces the centrality of governance by <7>design</7> for the legal and consumer-law qualification of the problem <8>Mucelin</8><9>(Marques; Mucelin, 2022, p. 16)</9>. Likewise, in treating successive-performance digital contracts as relationships driven by the search for security, future performance, status or a certain quality, and in describing the position of dependence as captivity in the context of current relationships, the author offers a dogmatic point of support to articulate permanence, exit cost and expectation of quality as elements inherent to the integrity of continuous consumption <10>Mucelin</10><11>(Marques; Mucelin, 2022, p. 23-24)</11>. The objective, therefore, is not to replace the grammar of the CDC with an environmental label, but to bring these mechanisms back to criteria of quality and protection of integrity, preserving the instrumental character of the vocabulary and preparing the critique of the expression digital vulnerability as a polysemic category that tends to describe the scenario more than the operator of power. <12>↩</12>

<1>Open auditability</1>
<1>Functional value equivalence</1>

Platform-governed enjoyment already makes it possible to keep the immaterial object of consumption intelligible in the vocabulary of the CDC without reducing supply to the inaugural instant or dissolving what was acquired into undifferentiated performance. Even so, the most sensitive dogmatic friction appears when utility depends on continuous modulations operated under technical opacity, so that relevant alterations occur without a single event, without verifiable justification and without a common language to compare promise, performance and reconfiguration. The frustration of the enjoyment bundle tends, then, to present itself as noise, and the legal response oscillates between two equally unproductive extremes: requiring total transparency incompatible with the functioning of the technical-organizational environment or accepting mutability as a neutral datum, normalizing substantial degradations as mere operational variation.

The problem does not lie in prohibiting evolution or in denying technical complexity. The problem lies in setting minimum criteria that make the governance of supply verifiable and decidable when the object is realized as a position of enjoyment over time. This requirement can be condensed into two complementary operators. Open auditability designates the minimum level of external verifiability capable of transforming opaque modulations into matter susceptible to adversarial proceedings, proof and decision. Functional value equivalence designates the criterion of comparison and restoration by which one judges whether the utility delivered, after relevant modulations, substantially preserves the core of enjoyed utility, including when part of the value is structured by socially verifiable symbolic dimensions. The first operator makes traceable what was altered and why. The second defines what must remain equivalent and what, when downgraded, requires a legal response compatible with continued enjoyment.

A technically simple and dogmatically expressive example of this requirement of equivalence appears in updates to visual effects on old cosmetics, carried out under the label of modernizing the game. In an environment in which enjoyment depends on visual signals, legibility and social recognition, the functional value of the cosmetic is not exhausted in its formal existence in the inventory. It includes the way the item presents itself in the game space, the clarity with which it communicates an ability, the consistency of the visual “weight” the user experiences when triggering effects, and also the public distinction that the cosmetic produces in <1>p. 470</1> comparison with common versions. When this set is persistently altered, equivalence is not resolved with the answer that the item “is still there”, because the core of enjoyed utility may have been reconfigured.

This problem does not transform every improvement into an unlawful act. Updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility in a competitive ecosystem. The relevant legal question arises when the adjustment, although justifiable under a systemic rationality, shifts enjoyment to a version that, for some consumers, no longer corresponds to what was economically stabilized at the moment of acquisition. In this scenario, auditability and equivalence operate together. Open auditability requires a verifiable narrative of what changed and by which criteria, while equivalence requires that the comparison be made by what matters for utility, and not by the generic rhetoric of “evolution”. This connection becomes even more sensitive when the contractual regime itself assumes mutability as the rule of the service, including with regard to virtual products and automatic adjustments made over time <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2><3><4>467</4></3>.

The point of contact with the practical life of the service is direct. The company itself states, in a public text, that these updates aim to improve legibility, reduce visual noise and order objectives by priority, even when this implies reducing fine details considered excessive, reorganizing hierarchies and favoring clarity over other aesthetic dimensions <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022a)</2><3><4>468</4></3>. In terms of institutional structure, this means that there is a declared teleology that guides the alteration. It is understandable and, from the standpoint of the <5>p. 471</5> ecosystem, may be desirable. What is lacking, from the standpoint of consumption, is a stable standard of comparison capable of recognizing when modernization alters what justified the price and the choice, especially in items whose value depends on the visual experience and on public distinction.

The practical insufficiency appears when the information made available to the consumer is, as a rule, narrative and dispersed. The typical public channel for recording changes to the game is the set of patch notes, published in regular cycles, which describe changes and communicate directions, but is not structured as a comparative mechanism aimed at the consumer who needs to demonstrate degradation of a specific visual utility over time <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]b)</2><3><4>469</4></3>. In an environment of high complexity, this creates a predictable imbalance. The platform holds the complete history of decisions, versions and criteria, while the consumer receives only communicational fragments, insufficient to sustain, in a common language, the comparison between the stabilized promise and the reconfigured delivery.

It is here that the legal response proposed by auditability and equivalence proves moderate and functional. It does not require freezing the service or prohibit updates. It requires an institutionally loyal way out when the platform makes a substantial change to a good acquired under a stable regime of enjoyment. If the alteration preserves the core of utility, performance continues. If the alteration relevantly downgrades what structured utility for that consumer, restoration must include, at least, mechanisms of choice that prevent captivity by surprise, with alternatives such as refund, credit, exchange for another cosmetic of equivalent value or analogous forms of recovering the investment for the consumer's reinsertion into the ecosystem, without requiring from them the impossible proof of a black box. This design keeps the dialogue open and preserves the possibility of modernization, while preventing “update” from functioning as a label to impose on the consumer a version that they had no reason to expect would be the new basis of enjoyment.

The methodological starting point of this construction lies in the replacement of the ideal of immovable fixation of meaning with a requirement of control criteria capable of operating under <1>p. 472</1> indeterminacy and complexity. It is in this sense that Humberto Ávila formulates an explicit turn by maintaining that the focus should be shifted from security of meaning to security of criteria, in order to provide, in advance, prior and abstract parameters to face later and concrete interpretive problems <2>Ávila</2><3>(Ávila, 2011, p. 71)</3>. The consequence is that the protection of the IOC does not depend on total transparency of the internal functioning of the platform, nor on absolute semantic certainty about each aspect of supply. It depends on conditions of intersubjective controllability capable of exposing reasons, delimiting objects of dispute and making argumentative reconstruction verifiable.

This requirement operates through determinability and relative certainty, not through the illusion of absolute determination. Ávila makes explicit that legal certainty depends on the capacity to understand the possible meanings of the normative text from cores of signification reconstructed through intersubjectively controllable argumentative processes, which grounds the notion of determinability and relative certainty of Law <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2011, p. 123)</2>. On the plane of argument, this functions as a lock against arbitrariness. In addressing the process of legal argumentation, the author states that certainty is based on intersubjectively controllable criteria and that, in this sense, it is, above all, rational control of argumentative arbitrariness <3>Ávila</3><4>(Ávila, 2011, p. 169)</4>. These statements authorize shifting the debate about platforms. The question is not to open the black box all the way, but to define prior and controllable criteria that make it possible to transform technically opaque modulations into legally decidable alternatives, without reducing control to automatic deference to complexity.

Open auditability, in this framework, designates a minimum requirement of verifiability applicable to supply when the acquired utility is realized as continued enjoyment governed by a platform. Its focus is not to produce full transparency of the technical-organizational environment or to impose complete disclosure of models, source code, proprietary metrics or trade secrets. What is at stake is a level of external intelligibility sufficient to reconstruct, in adversarial proceedings, the relation between promise, performance and modulation. This level must make it possible to identify what was altered, to what extent the alteration bore on the enjoyment bundle and which reasons were mobilized to justify it. In governed consumption, opacity is not an episodic anomaly; it is a structural condition of the mode of supply. Without a verifiable minimum, complexity becomes a shield, proof becomes asymmetrical to a radical degree and mutability tends to be trivialized as an “update”, even when the practical result is the persistent emptying of the core of utility.

<1>p. 473</1> The usefulness of the requirement becomes evident when frustration does not take the form of total interruption, but of partial degradations, gradual reconfigurations and cumulative restrictions that erode enjoyment without producing an unequivocal event. Open auditability prevents continued performance from becoming a legally unassessable gray zone. It is not a matter of requiring the consumer to fully understand the functioning of the system. It is a matter of ensuring sufficient verifiable elements to locate what was promised, what was actually delivered and what was later reconfigured by acts of maintenance, curation, updating, <2>enforcement</2> and management of conditions of access and use. Without this, the conflict migrates to the plane of the unsayable and produces two degenerative effects. The supplier comes to hold the practical monopoly of the “real”, and the consumer is reduced to a bearer of symptoms, without a common language that allows comparison and control.

This requirement also operates as a negative edge against two symmetrical excesses. On one side, it prevents legal control from getting lost in the pursuit of total transparency, converting the proceedings into a dispute about internal engineering, instead of the protection of consumption. On the other, it prevents the generic invocation of “internal policy”, “security”, “improvement of the service” or “integrity of the ecosystem” from functioning as a self-sufficient justification immune to control, emptying duties of information, loyalty and adequacy in continued performance. Open auditability is the level that shifts the discussion from “trust me” to the verifiable reconstruction of what was modulated, preparing the application of a second operator that judges equivalence and guides restoration.

The dogmatic justification of this cut does not depend on a promise of total technical truth. In Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr., modern dogmatics presents itself as a technology oriented toward action, and not as contemplation of the world. For this reason, “dogmatic technology” becomes an interpellation of social life, “forcing it”, “concealing it” and “manipulating it”, precisely to extract from it the maximum that is operable in the form of decision <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 80])</2>. The cut that dispenses with full transparency and, even so, requires minimum conditions of controllability is legitimized in this register. Law does not need to see everything in order to control. It needs to cut out what is relevant to make the conflict treatable, prevent opacity from functioning as shielding and allow the dispute to be organized in institutionally decidable terms.

This technological orientation is concretized in the form of doctrinal propositions, which offer schemes of orientation and technical rules. Ferraz Jr. describes this role by stating that such propositions take the form of “orientations”, as “schemes, systematizations”, or the form of “recommendations”, persuasive propositions that become rules of the type “if you want x, you must z” <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 79])</2>. Open auditability occupies this place in the IOC <3>p. 474</3> regime. It provides a scheme for reconstructing supply under opacity and a technical rule for transforming continuous modulation into verifiable criteria about what changed, how it changed and what impact was produced. The result is compatible with the institutional function of decision, which is to put an end to the conflict.

Ferraz Jr. observes that the institutionalization of conflict and of the decision-making procedure causes legal conflicts to “end”, in the sense that the decision puts an end to them by “preventing their continuation”, unlike social conflicts that may be resumed indefinitely <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 14])</2>. In platform-governed consumption, structural opacity tends to push the dispute toward interminability, because there always remains a technical “behind the scenes” that could explain the effect. A minimum level of auditability operates as a mechanism of finitude, organizing the debate around elements that can be reconstructed and discussed in adversarial proceedings, without the fiction of total transparency.

The same logic is reinforced when control is understood as programming oriented toward conditions and means. Ferraz Jr. observes that, in conditional programming, the decision-maker's responsibility is for the “correct use and exploitation of the means”, and that the prevalence of this programming makes the legal decision a procedure in which care with formal practices and control criteria gains relevance <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 315])</2>. Faced with complex and mutable systems, protection does not depend on knowing all the variables of the ecosystem. It depends on operating through controllable conditions, that is, through verifiable criteria that make it possible to assess the correctness of the modulation procedure, the sufficiency of the reasons presented and the causal link between alteration and degradation of the enjoyment bundle. Open auditability thus ceases to be a generic appeal for transparency and becomes a dogmatic instrument of decidability.

Platform governance does not function as a neutral background. It organizes the space of enjoyment and defines, in practice, who enters, who stays, under what conditions and by which mechanisms someone is contained or excluded. Julie E. Cohen describes this power in treating dominant platforms as agents capable of producing and controlling a type of territory of their own, which is not physical, but is constructed by protocols, data flows and algorithms, and which presents itself to the user as a space demarcated and protected by guarded borders <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 235)</2>. If enjoyment happens within this algorithmic territory, one cannot depend on intuition about what occurs behind the service. The border of authorization itself is already part of the mode of supply. For this reason, open auditability appears as a minimum condition to map, in verifiable terms, the operational rules that configure the space of enjoyment and the reasons that justify its alteration.

<1>p. 475</1> This cartography is indispensable because the apparent flexibility of the environment is managed by architectural mechanisms that selectively enable certain choices and block others. Cohen states that platform protocols impose a modular structure that enables certain kinds of flexibility and, at the same time, blocks others <2>Cohen</2><3>(Cohen, 2019, p. 42)</3>. She adds that control through protocols also enables intermediation and favors legibility, making it possible for the platform to operate according to its own priorities <4>Cohen</4><5>(Cohen, 2019, p. 42)</5>. Without minimum auditability, what modularity executes remains invisible while the user's experience is presented as free choice. The proposed requirement does not eliminate complexity. It prevents the invisibility of selective blocks from becoming practical immunity of the supplier, especially when changes of protocol, curation or legibility criteria reconfigure the enjoyment bundle.

This requirement is reinforced when one recognizes that the platform not only records data, but manufactures operational representations of users to make behavior calculable, predictable and economically exploitable at scale <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 67)</2>. In this scenario, treating opacity as something neutral amounts to normalizing modulation as an ordinary and uncontestable form of governance of supply. Open auditability provides the minimum necessary so that decisions of curation, <3>ranking</3>, access, participation and sanction can be reconstructed and discussed in adversarial proceedings when they interfere relevantly with enjoyment over time. Cohen herself formulates the need for this level by maintaining that algorithms and protocols classify subjects, shape information flows and authorize or deny access to network resources, so that any meaningful control of the surroundings depends on a baseline level of information about what these mechanisms do <4>Cohen</4><5>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 189])</5>. Open auditability is anchored precisely in this baseline level.

On the plane of operative translation, open auditability is expressed as a standard of verifiable reasoning applicable to the relevant modulations of supply in continued enjoyment. When the platform alters access rules, reconfigures functionalities, imposes selective frictions, reorganizes regimes of visibility, applies sanctions, modifies curation parameters or carries out cumulative restrictions that substantially affect the enjoyed utility, it is not enough to invoke generalities. The reasoning needs to offer sufficient elements to reconstruct the link between change and the affected enjoyment bundle, allowing the consumer to understand what occurred, delimit the object of the conflict and submit the justification to adversarial scrutiny without depending on total technical knowledge of the system. This minimum level can be described by the identification of the act of modulation and of the temporality of its effects, by the indication of the functional impact on practical dimensions of enjoyment, by the statement of operational reasons <1>p. 476</1> with purpose and criteria of application and by the indication of means of contestation and review. The effect is to shift the controversy from the plane of the unsayable narrative to the plane of a verifiable reconstruction, without turning every adjustment into litigation and without requiring exhaustive explanation.

The requirement gains institutional density when private governance is recognized as effective normativity. In Eros Roberto Grau, the contractual relationship is described as the expression of an economic relationship that, whether or not legally regulated, already operates as a relationship of will, whose content is determined by the economic relationship itself <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 61)</2>. Recognizing this normativity does not amount to accepting it as destiny. Grau formulates a two-way street by stating that presupposed law springs from society and conditions the elaboration of posited law, but that positive law, when it applies, modifies presupposed law <3>Grau</3><4>(Grau, 2008, p. 64)</4>. On platforms, terms, protocols, flows and <5>enforcement</5> establish a practical order that organizes expectations and distributes positions. Open auditability functions as a technique for bringing this established order back to the plane of the controllable, without purporting to fully inspect the technical design, but preventing the exercise of power from becoming immune to verification.

This organized coercion is precisely the trait that makes control legally unavoidable. In discussing the formation of the rule of law from Duguit, Grau indicates that a social norm becomes a legal norm when the mass of consciences understands that the sanction can be “socially organized” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 73)</2>. On platforms, the sanction materializes in suspension, banning, downgrading of visibility, blocking of functionalities, restrictions on participation and multiple forms of automated or hybrid sanction, executed by architecture and by internal procedures. When sanctions and restrictions operate as a pattern, governance ceases to be mere advice and comes to function as an effective normative regime. The demand for auditability is not an aesthetic agenda of transparency, but a minimum requirement for submitting private coercion to rational control. The same intuition appears when Grau observes that the market posits its legal order by establishing an order produced by it <3>Grau</3><4>(Grau, 2008, p. 326)</4>. If an order is established and applied by organized coercion, the minimum that can be required for decidability and legitimacy is that relevant decisions be reconstructible, contestable and assessable by objective criteria.

Once this level is established, the debate changes in nature. The dispute ceases to be about what the system did and comes to be about what must remain equivalent in continuous supply. It is here that the second operator comes in. Functional value equivalence is not a promise of freezing supply or a right to an eternal version of the service. It is the criterion of substantial preservation of the core of enjoyed utility in an <1>p. 477</1> intrinsically reconfigurable environment. In continued enjoyment, changes of means, method, architecture and execution may be legitimate, including for reasons of security, stability and compatibility. The limit is that these changes cannot substantially and persistently downgrade the enjoyment bundle for which the consumer kept paying, or turn adaptation into an alibi for emptying utility.

This criterion also operates through negative edges. Mere aesthetic preference for an old experience is not equivalence, nor is nonconformity with ordinary variations of the service. Equivalence is not the measure of internal states, feelings or psychological accounts of the consumer. The comparison is made by substantial preservation of functions and of positions of use that structure utility, including instrumental and symbolic dimensions when these are a constitutive and socially verifiable part of enjoyment in the ecosystem. It is precisely for this reason that equivalence requires, as a precondition, the level of auditability: without traceability of changes, without indication of impacts and without explicit criteria of application, there is no rational basis for comparing promise and delivery and for distinguishing legitimate adaptation from emptying reconfiguration.

Functional value equivalence, when applied to symbolic components of the enjoyment bundle, requires a lock against psychologism. In Eco, the symbolic dimension of value can be treated as a stabilized cultural correlation, and not as a private mental state. Thus, the objection of mentalism does not hold because one is not speaking of associations or mental images, but of correlations formulated in cultural terms, which refer to one another on an abstractly cultural plane, regardless of whether a human mind carries out this association <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 2000, p. 163)</2>. This makes it possible to reconstruct the symbolic as an objective datum of the system, and not as an intimate phenomenon.

Objectivity stems from the socially coercive character of the code. Eco describes the linguistic code as something established by social crystallization, the product of a statistical average fixed by use and which, once stabilized, comes to operate with coercive value, imposing a system of relations that speakers obey, often unconsciously <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 1997, p. 31)</2>. In digital ecosystems, signs, metrics, badges, rarities, <3>rankings</3> and regimes of visibility do not function as a subjective ornament added to the “real product”. They operate as coercive relations of the environment of enjoyment itself, to which the consumer is subjected through participation.

The same logic prevents treating connotation as an unpredictable nebula. Eco indicates that there are diffuse subcodes that authorize specific connotations and observes that, in certain semantic subuniverses, widely authorized connotations and axiological <1>p. 478</1> marks fall upon a term, guiding predictable readings <2>Eco</2><3>(Eco, 2000, p. 162)</3>. The consequence, for equivalence, is that symbolic losses can be described by public criteria. The expectation is not idiosyncratic, but authorized and induced by code.

Eco maintains that cultural units are semiotic postulates and that the ordinary producer of signs does not see them, but uses them, while a theory of signs does not use them, but sees them <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 2000, p. 120)</2>. The perspective is methodologically decisive because it makes it possible to make visible, by public criteria, the rule of cultural equivalence that the consumer merely practices. Accordingly, functional value equivalence admits a controllable symbolic axis, capable of comparing what was stabilized in the system of signs with what came to be delivered after reconfigurations, including in regimes of visibility, belonging and distinction.

Once such a limit is fixed, functional value equivalence can be formulated as a criterion of comparison between the utility stabilized in the bond and the utility delivered after relevant modulations. Continued performance may justify adjustments and updates, but does not authorize the platform to preserve formal access and structurally degrade the practical content of enjoyment through silent substitution of functionalities, introduction of selective frictions, persistent reduction of reach and visibility, reordering that disfigures reputation criteria or imposition of barriers that make permanence economically or socially innocuous. Equivalence functions as a yardstick of relevance, since it transforms the discussion about change into a discussion about preservation of the core, distinguishing ordinary variation from substantial and persistent downgrading.

Consumer-law dogmatics offers direct support for this criterion because it abandons the static view of the bond and treats the contract as a process. Claudia Lima Marques states that the contract must be viewed as a dynamic relationship, which is born, lives and dies, configuring a true process that unfolds over time and radiates legal effects during its performance, before it and after it <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 222-223)</2>. If the contract is a process, equivalence does not require identity of means. It requires substantial continuity of the expected core of utility, especially when utility depends on a technical-organizational environment in continuous operation.

This premise prevents treating the interval of performance as a neutral zone. Marques rejects the idea of an empty space between the birth of the obligation and the satisfaction of the main performance, by stating that the obligational relationship is a continuous whole. In this dynamic, from the birth of the relationship, and even before, the parties are already bound by ancillary duties of conduct, imposed by good faith in performance <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 110)</2>. In platform-governed enjoyment, <3>p. 479</3> preserving functional equivalence frequently requires active conduct over time, and not mere formal conservation of access.

The very structure of long-term contracts reinforces that adaptability is an expected component of the bond, but under a horizon of trust and maintenance of quality. Marques describes these contracts as based “more on trust, on reiterated interaction, on the maintenance of the economic potential and the quality of services”, as carrying “the implicit expectation of changes in social, economic and legal conditions”, and concludes that “the capacity for adaptation, for cooperation between contracting parties, for continuation of the contractual relationship is here essential, basic” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 74)</2>. This formulation provides the fine fit for functional value equivalence: changes may be admissible and even necessary, provided they are oriented toward maintaining the potential and the quality that structure the enjoyed utility, and not toward the silent substitution of the object by a less valuable version.

The point is completed with the creative function of objective good faith as a source of new duties and of liability for professional risks that cannot be disposed of by contract. Marques, Benjamin and Miragem record that good faith performs a creative function, as a source of new ancillary duties and also as a source of liability for lawful acts “by imposing new professional risks now not disposable by contract” (2013, p. 235). The consequence is evident, since, if continued performance exposes the consumer to risks of technical obsolescence, compatibility mutations and structural reconfigurations, good faith must require care, cooperation and maintenance as duties of preservation of functional equivalence, and thus impose liability when trust is broken by reconfigurations that relevantly and persistently degrade the core of utility.

Functional value equivalence also requires an objective lock against the attempt to legitimize unilateral downgrading as “evolution of the service”. In contracts of continuous performance, permanence is the mode of existence of the bond. Rizzatto Nunes describes these contracts as relationships whose “characteristic” is continuity <1>ad infinitum</1> while the consumer fulfills the obligation to pay, the indeterminacy of the term being the central trait <2>Nunes</2><3>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508])</3>. If continuity is the normal regime, the enjoyed utility stabilizes as an expectation of maintenance of the level of delivery, and not as an expectation of formal access to a service that may be reconfigured at the supplier's convenience. For this reason, the CDC treats unilateral modification of content or quality as a ground of nullity. In commenting on <4>p. 480</4> Article 51, item XIII<5><6>470</6></5>, Nunes asks, in a deliberately frontal way, how it would be possible to unilaterally alter a contract and, even so, confer legal validity on the alteration <7>Nunes</7><8>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508-509])</8>. The example he offers, of the supplier that reduces classes while keeping the same price <9>Nunes</9><10>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508-509])</10>, functions as an objective yardstick for platforms. The reduction rarely appears as an explicit cut of “classes”, but may manifest itself as loss of reach, persistent downgrading of performance, cumulative restriction of functionalities, compression of limits, reordering of visibility or structural alterations that raise the cost of enjoying the same utility. The logic is the same. The label and the price are kept, and the delivery of value is downgraded.

With this, functional value equivalence stabilizes as an internal limit on adaptation in continued enjoyment. Changes of means and method may be legitimate, and sometimes necessary, to keep supply viable. The limit is that they cannot be used to shift structural risks onto the consumer, degrade quality, restrict relevant functionalities, erode conditions of access or reconfigure regimes of participation and recognition that were part of the economically stabilized enjoyment. Whenever the platform invokes “update”, “adjustment” or “evolution of the service” to justify persistent alterations, the core of the debate must turn on demonstrating the substantial preservation of the enjoyment bundle, and not on the rhetoric of complexity.

This point requires a methodological basis for rejecting general labels that erase functional distinctions. Larenz points out that abbreviated formulas may serve external systematics, but are not an adequate basis for arguing about content and limits, precisely because they tend to obliterate distinctions oriented by social reality and by function when one operates only with a general and abstract concept <1>Larenz</1><2>(Larenz, 1997, p. 317)</2>. In platform-governed enjoyment, reducing the IOC to “service” in a generic sense may work as an external label, but fails where dogmatics needs to work, namely in defining content, limits and criteria of comparison. The answer to this erasure is neither to inflate categories nor to replace dogmatics with moral indignation. What is required is to rebuild the boundaries through functional distinctions anchored in an explicit evaluative point of view. In this sense, for Larenz, real-normative types and legal-structural types do not hold without this guiding evaluative point of view. He shows by example how certain legal connections depend on the relation between self-interest and risk <3>Larenz</3><4>(Larenz, 1997, p. 308-309)</4>. Under governed consumption, there is a coupling <5>p. 481</5> between the supplier's interest in governing the environment and the typical risk of discontinuity, modulation and downgrading of enjoyment, a risk that needs to be recognized and controlled in continued supply.

This movement also protects the construction against the objection of “invention” of Law, because the legal system is open and requires functional concretization when the factual basis shifts. Larenz describes the system as an “‘open’ and, to a certain degree, ‘mobile’ system”, always incomplete and continually called into question, whose function is to make clear the “intrinsic rationality”, the guiding values and the principles of Law <1>Larenz</1><2>(Larenz, 1997, p. 241)</2>. If technology shifts the mode of realization of consumption, preserving the internal rationality of the CDC requires concretization through functional distinctions. Open auditability and functional value equivalence occupy this place: they do not replace the system; they allow it to see, by controllable criteria, what abbreviated formulas tend to erase.

The attempt to condition the legal control of opaque ecosystems on total transparency misses the target and produces paralysis. In an ideal scenario in which “all relevant data would be known from the outset” and “all alternatives could be enumerated and evaluated”, there would remain “only the choice”, but this scenario does not describe the real legal decision, which operates where information is incomplete and premises are uncertain, having as its immediate purpose the absorption of insecurity <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 43)</2>.
